plan: Expression of Ideas weighted up; first poetry-quotation evidence item; method-plus-limitation synthesis; cross-text with a mechanism contradiction; parentheses and finite-verb conventions.

passages.title: Committee response
passages.text: The committee's response to the proposal was notably ______: it neither endorsed nor rejected the plan, instead requesting another year of study before taking any position.

passages.title: Lamplighter poem
passages.text: In the poem "The Lamplighter," the speaker presents the lamplighter as both solitary and essential to the life of the town.

passages.title: Algae timing
passages.text: Some ecologists have proposed that a lake's algae blooms are caused mainly by fertilizer runoff from nearby farms. If that were the case, the largest blooms would be expected soon after heavy spring rains, when runoff peaks. Instead, six years of monitoring show that the largest blooms occur in late summer, during the driest weeks of the year, months after runoff has peaked. This pattern suggests that ______

passages.title: Learning grammar (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A linguist argues that young children learn the grammar of their first language mainly because adults correct their grammatical mistakes.

Text 2
Researchers who recorded hundreds of hours of conversation between parents and young children found that parents rarely corrected grammatical errors; they usually corrected statements that were factually wrong instead. The children nevertheless acquired their language's grammar on a typical schedule.

passages.title: Old library
passages.text: Founded in 1891 with a collection of just four hundred books, the city library ______ more than two million volumes today, many of them donated by local families.

passages.title: Bridge designer
passages.text: The bridge's designer (a self-taught engineer who had never ______ was praised by critics who had predicted that the span would collapse within a decade.

passages.title: Recycling program
passages.text: The city's new recycling program collected far more material than officials had expected in its first year. ______ much of that material could not actually be recycled, because residents often placed food-soiled containers in their bins.

passages.title: Commute notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Researchers studied 1,200 commuters in three cities.
• Participants recorded every commute in a phone app for four weeks.
• Commutes by bicycle were the most predictable in duration.
• All three cities in the study have flat terrain.

passages.title: Mural notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Artist Tomás Reyes painted the mural River Voices in 2019.
• The mural covers one side of a grain silo.
• It is 40 meters tall and 25 meters wide.
• It took Reyes 14 months to complete.
• It depicts people who once worked on the river.

passages.title: Toy collection
passages.text: The museum's new wing, which opened last spring, is devoted entirely to ______ toys from the nineteenth century, including dolls, tin soldiers, and hand-carved wooden animals.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it neither endorsed nor rejected the plan
candidates.explanation: A response that neither endorses nor rejects and defers a decision is noncommittal: "equivocal."

A.rationale: An emphatic response takes a strong position; the committee took none.

B.rationale: A hostile response opposes the plan, but the committee did not reject it.

D.rationale: Unanimity describes agreement among members, not the content of the response.

hints: What does the clause after the colon say the committee did?
candidates.remember: The colon clause defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "He walks alone where no one waits for him, / and every window brightens as he goes."
choices.B: "The evening settles slowly on the square, / and shutters close along the empty street."
choices.C: "His ladder leans against the iron post; / he climbs, and strikes the match, and climbs back down."
choices.D: "The children call to one another, laughing, / and run indoors before the light is gone."

candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts. "Walks alone where no one waits for him" shows solitude; "every window brightens as he goes" shows his importance to the town.

B.rationale: This describes the setting, not the lamplighter.

C.rationale: This describes his routine but shows neither his solitude nor his importance.

D.rationale: This describes other people, not the lamplighter.

strategy.explanation: Turn the claim into two things to look for.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: fertilizer runoff has no effect of any kind on the amount of algae in the lake.
choices.B: spring rains in the region grew steadily heavier over the six years of monitoring.
choices.C: the farms near the lake stopped using fertilizer at some point during the study.
choices.D: something other than runoff, such as warm late-summer water, may matter more.

candidates.explanation: The blooms peak when runoff is lowest, which contradicts the prediction of the runoff explanation and points to another, timing-related factor.

A.rationale: The timing weakens runoff as the main cause; it does not show runoff has no effect.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests farms changed their practices.

hints: What did the runoff explanation predict?
Did the data match the prediction?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that overstate or go beyond the data.

candidates.remember: A failed prediction weakens a claim without disproving every part of it.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the linguist's claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By noting that children master grammar even though they seldom receive the correction the claim relies on
choices.B: By agreeing that adult corrections are the main source of children's grammatical knowledge
choices.C: By arguing that correcting a child's factual errors is more harmful than correcting grammar
choices.D: By suggesting that children who are corrected more often learn grammar more slowly than others

candidates.explanation: If grammatical corrections are rare yet children still learn grammar on schedule, correction cannot be the main mechanism, contradicting Text 1.

B.rationale: Their findings show such corrections are rare, which undercuts the claim.

C.rationale: Text 2 makes no claim about harm.

D.rationale: Text 2 does not compare children by how often they are corrected.

hints: What does Text 1 say causes grammar learning?
How common is that cause, according to Text 2?

strategy.explanation: Compare the claimed cause with the observed frequency.

candidates.remember: If the supposed cause is rare, the effect needs another explanation.

candidates.subskill: Finite verb in a main clause
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Founded in 1891 with a collection of just four hundred books, the city library
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase modifies "the city library," which needs a main verb; "today" calls for the present tense "holds."

A.rationale: "Holding" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

B.rationale: "To hold" is not a finite verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.rationale: "Having held" is a participle and leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: Does the sentence already have a main verb?
candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a finite main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: built a structure longer than fifty meters)
choices.B: built a structure longer than fifty meters),
choices.C: built a structure longer than fifty meters—
choices.D: built a structure longer than fifty meters

candidates.explanation: The aside opens with a parenthesis, so it must close with one; no comma belongs between the subject "designer" and the verb "was praised."

B.rationale: A comma after the closing parenthesis would separate the subject from its verb "was praised."

C.rationale: An opening parenthesis must be closed with a parenthesis, not a dash.

D.rationale: Without a closing parenthesis, the aside never ends.

hints: What is the main verb of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Match the closing mark to the opening mark.

candidates.remember: Close what you open; keep subject and verb together.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: collected far more material than officials had expected
candidates.explanation: The first sentence reports apparent success; the second reveals a problem with it. "However" marks the contrast.

A.rationale: The second sentence is not similar to the first; it qualifies its success.

B.rationale: "Moreover" adds a further point in the same direction, but this one undercuts the first.

D.rationale: Unrecyclable material is not a result of collecting a lot of material.

hints: Does the second sentence support or undercut the first?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship before choosing a transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to describe the study's method while acknowledging a limitation of its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Among the 1,200 commuters studied, trips by bicycle were the most predictable in duration overall.
choices.B: Commuters in three flat cities logged trips in an app for four weeks, so results may differ in hilly places.
choices.C: Researchers studied 1,200 commuters, who each recorded every commute in a phone app for four weeks.
choices.D: Because the cities studied were all flat, bicycle trips may be far less predictable in hilly regions.

candidates.evidence: All three cities in the study have flat terrain.
candidates.explanation: The goal has two parts: method (app logging over four weeks) and a limitation (only flat cities). B gives both.

A.rationale: This states a finding, with no method or limitation.

C.rationale: This describes the method but acknowledges no limitation.

D.rationale: This gives a limitation but does not describe the method.

strategy.explanation: Make a two-item checklist from the goal.

candidates.remember: Every part of the goal must be met.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize the size of River Voices. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Tomás Reyes's mural River Voices depicts people who once worked on the river.
choices.B: River Voices, a mural by Tomás Reyes, took 14 months to complete, ending in 2019.
choices.C: Tomás Reyes painted River Voices on the side of a grain silo in 2019.
choices.D: Covering one side of a grain silo, River Voices is 40 meters tall and 25 meters wide.

candidates.evidence: It is 40 meters tall and 25 meters wide.
candidates.explanation: Only D gives the mural's dimensions, which directly convey its size.

A.rationale: This describes the subject, not the size.

B.rationale: Time spent is not the same as physical size.

C.rationale: This mentions the silo but gives no dimensions.

strategy.explanation: Match the goal word "size" to the notes.

candidates.remember: Match the goal to the specific note.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: "Children" is an irregular plural, so its possessive adds 's: "children's."

A.rationale: "Children" is already plural, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

C.rationale: This has no apostrophe to show possession.

D.rationale: This adds an extra, unnecessary apostrophe.

strategy.explanation: Form the plural first, then add the possessive.

candidates.remember: Irregular plurals take 's in the possessive.
